summary: This RFC proposes rules for converting mail between the conventions of different message systems, in particular how header fields and recipient addresses are handled. The aim was to let mail move between differently built systems without losing meaning.

eli5.summary: A translator rewrites a letter's envelope and heading so a different post office can understand it, while the message inside stays the same.

questions: how to convert mail headers between mail systems
how to translate mail between different standards
what is a canonical form in mail translation
how do mail gateways handle format differences
subtitle: Rules for translating mail between systems with different message formats.

tldr.problem: As networks with different mail standards joined the Internet, mail had to move between systems with incompatible header formats and address representations. Without agreed rules, translation would lose information or fail.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 886 proposes canonical forms: intermediate abstract representations that capture the essential meaning of fields, addresses, and dates. A munging agent translates from a source format to its canonical form, then from that form to the target format. This isolates translation rules between pairs of formats and ensures all information is preserved or lost consistently.
tldr.outcome: The memo provided the conceptual foundation for mail gateways that bridge standards, but does not itself specify how to translate between any two particular formats. Later RFCs and implementations would use these ideas to build gateways between the Internet, USENET, BITNET and other networks.

today: RFC 886 is a historic memo that laid conceptual groundwork for mail gateways. It was superseded by more specific standards for translating between particular pairs of message formats, but its principle of canonical forms remains useful for understanding how mail systems bridge different standards.

sections.title: Mail Translation Between Standards
sections.content:
RFC 886 addresses a practical problem: as the ARPA Internet connected to other networks like USENET and BITNET, mail had to flow across boundaries where the networks used different message standards. Although RFC 822 defines the standard for Internet mail, other networks might use older formats like RFC 733 or proprietary schemes. When mail crossed a boundary, it needed translation.

The memo is not a replacement for RFC 822 but rather a conceptual guide for building software that translates mail between standards. It describes the philosophy and rules that a 'munging agent'—a program or gateway that transforms messages—should follow to preserve meaning while converting format. Although written with RFC 822 and USENET in mind, the ideas apply to any pair of message standards.
sections.eli5: When a letter crosses from one mail system to another, its envelope and heading need to be rewritten so the new system understands it. This is about how to do that rewrite correctly.

sections.title: What Needs to Change
sections.content:
Message munging occurs at several levels. Field transformation happens when two standards convey the same idea with different field names—for example, RFC 822 uses the Resent- prefix where an older format used Remailed-. Value transformation converts structured components within a field, such as an address: RFC 822 uses the format local-part@domain while USENET uses user!route!host. Field/value combination handles cases where one standard expresses an idea with a single field while another needs multiple fields, or vice versa. Header ordering concerns standards that require fields in a specific sequence.

The RFC does not specify the exact transformation rules between two particular standards. Instead, it lays out the principles that any munging agent should follow, leaving the specific mappings to future RFCs or to implementors who know both standards.
sections.eli5: Mail headers have different parts: names (like 'From'), values (like 'john@example.com'), and order. When copying between systems, any of these might need to change.

sections.title: Canonical Forms as a Bridge
sections.content:
The central idea is canonical form: an abstract, minimal representation of an object that captures its complete meaning. For an address, the canonical form holds only the essential parts—local-part and domain in RFC 822 terms, or user and route in USENET terms. By translating through a canonical form, a munging agent can avoid directly converting between every pair of formats. Instead, it extracts meaning into the canonical form, then expresses that meaning in the target standard.

The RFC notes that canonical forms need not be strings; they are a conceptual tool. An implementation could represent them as data structures or abstract objects. The key is that they express the minimum information required to fully describe the meaning of an object, stripping away presentation details like comments, formatting, or abbreviated syntax.
sections.eli5: Imagine a translator who doesn't directly convert address A to address B. Instead, they extract what the address means ('send to person Jane at company XYZ') and then write that meaning in the new system's format.

sections.title: Translation Rules
sections.content:
When performing translation, munging agents must follow several rules. Preservation of information requires that all information in the source canonical form be preserved in the target, even if the two standards differ. If a standard cannot represent something—for example, if the target format has no group addressing concept—the agent may preserve the information in a comment. However, comments must still conform to the target syntax.

Re-formatting allows munging agents to reflow headers if the translated form would exceed line length limits (the RFC 822 standard suggests 65 or 72 characters per line), but only if munging actually occurred. A header that was not changed must not be refolded. Error recovery requires agents to handle malformed source messages gracefully: two new reserved fields, Illegal-Field and Illegal-Object, allow the agent to record problems. For instance, Illegal-Field captures a header line too malformed to parse, while Illegal-Object records a field that could be parsed but whose value cannot be translated.

Finally, munging agents may introduce a Received header to document the transformation. This traces the message's journey across boundaries and helps with debugging. The Received field should include the source domain, target domain, and the munging agent's identity in the 'with' clause.
sections.eli5: When translating, keep everything that matters. If something can't be translated, write it down. If the new format has weird rules, follow them. And if you change a message, leave a note saying you did it.

sections.title: What Munging Applies To
sections.content:
Not every field in a message needs munging; only semantically significant ones. The RFC defines a minimum list of munge-objects: address fields (From, Sender, Reply-To, To, cc, Bcc and their Resent- variants) and date fields (Date, Resent-Date). The list is extensible; implementors may add others as needed and register them with future RFC revisions.

If address munging is performed, then all addresses in all address header-lines must be munged—it is forbidden to munge some addresses but not others, as this could break a message's coherence. Similarly, if date munging occurs, all Date and Resent-Date fields must be fully munged. One field is always exempt: Received headers must never be modified, as they serve as a trace and audit log.
sections.eli5: Only certain parts of the header need to change: addresses and dates mostly. If you change any address, change every one. And never touch the 'Received' headers—they're a record of where the mail has been.
